articles.title: Some women in Canada are choosing fertility treatments to avoid passing down genetic mutations to their kids
articles.summary: Egg freezing is surging in Canada and genetic testing is one of the motivations. We spoke with a woman planning to freeze her eggs so she can test her embryos for the BRCA 1 gene mutation.

image.caption: Fertility doctor Sony Sierra is pictured in her egg freezing clinic in Toronto. She says conversations about fertility treatments have become more mainstream, but there is still a long way to go to make them accessible to everyone who wants them. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Health·New
Egg freezing is surging in Canada and genetic testing is one of the motivations. We spoke with a woman planning to freeze her eggs so she can test her embryos for the BRCA 1 gene mutation.
It's one of the reasons women who aren't ready to get pregnant are considering egg freezing
After Emma Clayton Jones learned she had a genetic mutation that put her at higher risk for some cancers, she started thinking about freezing her eggs.
"I've always known that when I want to start a family, there would be the option to freeze my eggs and then test the embryos," she told CBC News.

Clayton Jones has the BRCA 1 mutation, an inherited genetic change that raises the lifetime risk of developing various cancers, including breast and ovarian — and she doesn't want to pass it on to her future kids. By freezing her eggs, Clayton Jones can plan ahead by preserving her fertility, and later, creating embryos that will be tested for the same genetic mutation.
"After having a cancer scare myself, I thought, 'If I have the choice and the privilege to not put someone through it, I won't.'"
Why are more British Columbians freezing their eggs?
She isn't alone — more women across Canada are considering freezing their eggs, a procedure that's surging in popularity among those who can afford it.

Experts say most people freeze their eggs to preserve their fertility. After all, people are having children later, for reasons like career ambitions, relationship status and the rising cost of living.
But many women like Clayton Jones are also coming forward, too, hoping to plan their pregnancies in a way that better protects their future children.
Ethical concerns

Egg freezing isn't absolutely necessary to pursue genetic testing, as it is the embryos, not the eggs themselves, that get tested. But it's a common path for women who have concerns about passing down health issues and who are unsure of when they want to have children. Once they are ready, they will often begin in vitro fertilization, or IVF.

"Testing embryos for genetic abnormalities is a safer and more reliable option, particularly given that sperm can also carry abnormalities," said Judith Daniluk, a University of British Columbia professor who specializes in women's fertility.

Experts warn there are some ethical concerns with genetic testing — particularly if it's done for reasons other than potential health issues, like sex selection. There are also some religious groups who believe that genetic testing is always morally wrong.

"Some disability advocates are also concerned about the slippery slope of trying to eliminate normal diversity within the human species," she said, "as well as further stigmatizing those with disabilities."
'Overall, it is still an uphill battle to make it accessible to anyone who wants to do it,' Dr. Sony Sierra said of fertility treatments and access to them. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Notably, it's a criminal offence in Canada to choose an embryo based on sex, unless it's to prevent a sex-linked illness, or to pursue so-called "designer babies," which have genetic traits selected for them that their parents consider desirable. Anyone found guilty faces a fine of up to $500,000 and up to 10 years in prison, though there have been no documented convictions of elective sex selection in Canada.

But in the U.S., where elective sex selection is legal, genetic testing has allowed people to choose whether their embryo will develop into a boy or a girl, said Caitlin Dunne, a reproductive endocrinologist and infertility specialist at the B.C.-based Pacific Centre for Reproductive Medicine.

Still, genetic testing for health reasons is legal in Canada. But fertility treatments aren't cheap. When it comes to egg freezing, doctors who spoke to CBC News said that one cycle typically costs around $8,000, with another $2,000 to $8,000 for medication.
Patients often need two or three cycles to increase their chances for pregnancy, and there are additional costs associated with storage.

Public funding for fertility treatments, such as in vitro fertilization, or IVF, varies from province to province and generally doesn't cover elective egg freezing. But increasingly, workplace benefits will cover a cycle, or at least the medication required for it.
Clayton Jones said she's still trying to figure out the costs.
A still image of Dr. Sierra's egg freezing clinic. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
The 32-year-old says she's thinking about pregnancy in the "next couple of years," but wants to balance her expectations with the cost of the procedure.
"It seems like it's going to be a bit of a patchwork of expenses. I'm trying to get to the bottom of how much to actually budget for something like this."
Fertility a 'public health concern' affecting many

"The egg freezing is more precipitated for me by the idea that I'd like to do the genetic testing of the embryos," Clayton Jones said. "I feel a tiny crunch of pressure related to the BRCA gene, but I am also trying to be cost-conscious."

Dr. Sony Sierra, Toronto-based medical director of Evolve Egg Freezing Clinic, told CBC News that elective egg freezing has become more popular and accessible because public discourse and celebrity stories have made it mainstream — but there is still a long way to go.
"Overall, it is still an uphill battle to make it accessible to anyone who wants to do it," she said, adding she hopes that improves over time.
Dunne says she also hopes fertility treatments will become more accessible as more people become informed.

"Look at your nieces or employees, sisters, aunts, people with ovaries. There are all kinds of people around you dealing with infertility or concerns. It truly is a public health concern that touches so many."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Anya Zoledziowski is a Peabody-winning multimedia journalist from Edmonton who's covered social and climate justice, Indigenous affairs, gender, politics and more, and has been recognized by several national and international awards. She’s currently pursuing her PhD in journalism studies.

articles.title: Veterans, families call for better access to make claims for exposure-related illness
articles.summary: A new report calls for the federal government to make it easier for service members and others exposed to health risks to find the information they need when making medical claims.

image.caption: A new report calls for the federal government to make it easier for service members and others exposed to health risks to find the information they need when making medical claims. (James Maclennan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
A new report calls for the federal government to make it easier for service members and others exposed to health risks to find the information they need when making medical claims.
Report recommends evidence be made more accessible to support medical claims
Hakan Haytaoglu was a military pilot who worked secret missions for the Canadian Armed Forces during his 35-year career.
At the age of 55, just months shy of retirement, he was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of cancer called neuroendocrine carcinoma.
He sought support through a medical claim to Veterans Affairs Canada, but the claim was denied.
Haytaoglu decided to appeal.
Hakan Haytaoglu was a pilot with the Canadian Armed Forces until his diagnosis with an aggressive cancer. His wife fought for medical benefits and won. (Submitted by Maura-Jo Haytaoglu)
For months, while caring for her dying husband, Maura-Jo Haytaoglu hunted down the evidence he needed to connect his illness to his job.
"I dug and I dug while he was sick in bed," she said. "I sat beside him and I researched and I dug and I put the proper people in my corner that fought for us."
The military pilot who friends and family called Hawk died just a few weeks before his case could be heard before the Veterans Review and Appeal Board in August 2025.
So Maura-Jo did it for him, and won.
"It was the hardest day of my entire life, beyond watching my husband die in my arms," Haytaoglu said.
"It shouldn't be this hard for those who served their country."

Maura-Jo Haytaoglu and husband Hakan as he received chemo treatments following his diagnosis of a rare cancer. He died in July 2025, just a few weeks shy of the appeal of his medical claim. (Submitted by Maura-Jo Haytaoglu)
A new report by the House of Commons national defence committee states there are 2,750 Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces contaminated sites in Canada as of June 2026.

Among 11 recommendations, the report calls for the federal government to make it easier for service members and others exposed to health risks to find the information they need when making medical claims.
CBC News reached out to Veterans Affairs Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces for reaction to the call for more access, and did not hear back in time for publication.
Invisible crisis
The report cites witness testimony by veterans like Erin Zimmerman.
Zimmerman has been helping more than two dozen veterans and their families locate evidence to support appeals for medical claims, including the Haytaoglu case.

Zimmerman says her expertise in research as a civil servant came in handy in her own fight for answers. The 48-year-old mother of four has been diagnosed with a rare form of early-onset Parkinson's disease. She worked at CFB Moose Jaw in sections now an active contamination site, including during one of her pregnancies.
She said she had never been informed of the risks.
Some of Erin Zimmerman's committee testimony was included in the final report released in October. (Submitted by Erin Zimmerman)
Zimmerman is grateful to see her calls for more transparency in the committee report.

One of its recommendations suggests the federal government "proactively inform personnel and families currently and previously living and/or working on Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces sites, bases and wings of environmental risks and assessment results."
"We're in a crisis," Zimmerman said. "But this crisis is an invisible demographic."
Veterans face significant difficulty obtaining reliable information about past toxic exposures, according to Jim Hutton with Veterans with Cancer Inc.
The non-profit works with veterans diagnosed with cancer to establish the connection between their service and their illness to back medical claims.
At the same time, Hutton said, Veterans Affairs does not properly track exposure-related cancer claims.
He said this leads to veterans having to file access to information requests and searching old government records, in multiple databases, to prove the risk they faced while serving their country.
"Veterans should not have to become investigators," Hutton said in an email to CBC News. "That is an unreasonable burden."

items: 20 years of pain: A woman veteran’s search for answers
Small actions go a long way to honour Indigenous veterans

blocks.text: The group documented cases where veterans failed to find the evidence they need because historical exposure information is missing, or can't be found in their military service records.
On the upside, once the evidence is found, it can help others who worked alongside that service member. That's what happened in Hawk Haytaoglu's case.
Maura-Jo Haytaoglu said the information used in her husband's successful appeal is now helping the surviving service members that worked with him on a secret mission some 30 years ago.
"Three of them are dead because of cancer, one is battling Stage 4 cancer and one has beat cancer three times," she said.
The surviving members used the precedent in their own claims.
"My husband's legacy lives on because we had the courage to say no, we're not going to accept this."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Amanda Pfeffer has worked for the CBC across the country, including Montreal, Vancouver, Fredericton, Quebec City and Ottawa. She welcomes story ideas and tips at amanda.pfeffer@cbc.ca, or twitter @onthebeat1.

articles.title: Suspicious tree removal and permits linked to Toronto developer
articles.summary: A Toronto developer is facing new accusations of illegal tree removal at a residential property in Etobicoke. Four trees were recently cut down without permits at a property connected to Modcity. The…

image.caption: A white fir at 65 Fortieth St. in Toronto's west end, described by locals as a staple of the community, was one of four trees in the neighbourhood recently cut down under suspicious circumstances. (Remax Hallmark Realty Ltd.)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A Toronto developer is facing new accusations of illegal tree removal at a residential property in Etobicoke. Four trees were recently cut down without permits at a property connected to Modcity. The company denies any wrongdoing.
Modcity denies any wrongdoing while city insists it didn't OK removals
A Toronto developer is facing new accusations of illegal tree removal at a residential property in the city's west end.
Modcity has faced numerous similar accusations in the past, and as of early September, the city had 10 open investigations related to the company.
Now, four more trees have been cut down without permits at a property connected to the company. This time, in the Long Branch neighbourhood of Etobicoke.
The affected trees include one that the city and locals previously fought to protect. The white fir towered above a two-bedroom bungalow, and had been the subject of neighbourhood walking tours.
"It was the epitome of the perfect tree," said neighbour Sherry McCutcheon.
Without it, the area is "bare … it's drab, it's very dreary looking now."

The loss of the white fir was "disturbing," said neighbour Randy McWatters, who says he remembers when it was not much taller than him. He'd watched it "grow and grow" for more than five decades, he said.
Several years ago, Randy McWatters was involved in a successful neighbourhood campaign to save the white fir at 65 Fortieth St. (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)
The incident also involves allegedly fraudulent tree removal permits.
The pattern of alleged wrongdoing is prompting calls for a harsher crackdown by the city and province. Modcity denies any wrongdoing.
Property tied to developer

The four trees were cut down at 65 Fortieth St. on Oct. 24. Property records show that was one day after the property changed hands, having been bought by a company directed by two of Modcity's co-founders: Ron Sheinin and Rohan Sadana.

CBC Toronto obtained photos of apparent removal permits for three trees in the backyard, which were posted at the property the day the trees were cut down. While the supposed permits have the City of Toronto letterhead, and list the address of the property, the city confirmed to CBC Toronto it did not issue them.
If the documents were forged, that would be a crime, says Amber Morley, the local city councillor.
"That needs to be fully investigated to the full extent of the law."
Morley says her office is working with city departments to explore options. The city confirmed it is investigating to determine if there were bylaw violations.
A violation could lead to proseuction, said media relations manager Kayla Lewis in an emailed statement.
City councillor Amber Morley says the possibility that forged permits were used must be 'fully investigated.' (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)

Sheinin and Sadana did not answer detailed questions from CBC Toronto, including whether they posted or authorized the posting of fake permits, or whether they authorized the removal of trees without city approval.
In an email, Sadana said they "strongly dispute" allegations of wrongdoing.

Several neighbours told CBC Toronto they saw Sheinin and Sadana at the property while the trees were being removed. A photo taken that same day also shows a car parked across the street with a Modcity vanity licence plate. The registered owner is a numbered company, of which Sheinin is the president and sole director.
Loss of beloved tree
The city and community had previously fought to protect that large white fir.

In 2018, the previous property owner applied to sever the property, with a plan to tear down the existing house and build two new ones. Toronto's committee of adjustment approved the application, despite objections from the city's urban forestry department.

The city ended up appealing the decision to the Toronto Local Appeal Body (TLAB), on the basis that the variances would require the removal of a healthy tree. The appeal was successful, with the TLAB issuing its decision in 2022.
Danijela Puric-Mladenovic of the University of Toronto says municipal bylaws aren't a strong enough tool to deter some developers from breaking the rules. (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)

It was a "nice tree, beautiful. And everybody commented on it all the time. So I'm sorry to see it go," said McWatters, who advocated to save the tree, including by gathering signatures from neighbours.
Danijela Puric-Mladenovic, an assistant professor in forestry at the University of Toronto, says losing large trees like that one is significant for the local environment.

"Whatever we plant will never reach the canopy that we used to have," Puric-Mladenovic said, "because there is no growing space. With those new developments, there is little place left for larger trees to develop."
Modcity is facing four charges related to tree bylaw offences, which are currently before the courts, and several other noise bylaw-related charges.

items: Developer under investigation after much-loved tree downed without permit
Accused of illegal tree-cutting again, Modcity faces 10th city investigation

blocks.text: The maximum fine for each offence is $100,000. However, under provincial legislation, the city cannot deny a developer a building permit on the basis of violating its tree bylaws.
Speaking generally, Puric-Mladenovic argued the potential fines aren't a strong enough deterrent, when compared with potential developer profits.

items: Police, city investigating tree removals without permit
Modcity again accused by neighbours of cutting trees without permits

blocks.text: "Even if they don't follow the rules, they know that that's not going to hurt them," she said.
Last year, the city asked the province to change the law, so that not complying with its tree bylaws would be grounds for denying a building permit.
The Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing has not responded to emails from CBC Toronto.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah MacMillan is a journalist with CBC Toronto. She previously reported in Sudbury, Ont., and Prince Edward Island. You can contact her at sarah.macmillan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Critics warn of health data privacy concerns as Ottawa ramps up AI strategy
articles.summary: The Canadian government wants to ramp up the development and adoption of AI systems, starting with the health sector, but experts warn that proposed measures to address privacy concerns have critical…

image.caption: As the federal government ramps up the development and adoption of AI systems, a new privacy bill aims to bring Canada's privacy regulations up to speed. But health experts warn that proposed measures to address privacy concerns have critical gaps, which run the risk of exposing sensitive personal h

blocks.text: Should a private company handling your personal health data be able to claim it has a “legitimate interest” that allows it to collect and use your information without your consent?
That’s just one of the concerns critics of Canada’s proposed privacy legislation are flagging in a recent commentary published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ).

This summer, the federal government announced an update to Canada’s private-sector privacy laws that would recognize privacy as a fundamental right, strengthen transparency around automated decisions by systems including AI, and allow individuals to request their personal information be deleted in certain circumstances.

Touted as a “key element” for Canada’s AI for All strategy, the federal government said in the announcement that the proposed bill will “establish clear guardrails to protect Canadians’ personal information in a rapidly changing digital world.”
But in the commentary, health researchers say Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, “contains critical gaps that leave sensitive health data exposed.”

Under the proposed law, private sector companies would be allowed to “collect, use or disclose an individual’s personal information without their knowledge or consent” provided they have a “legitimate interest” that outweighs any “reasonably foreseeable” harm to that individual.

“What's concerning about this is it's the company that's making the decision,” said Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a clinician scientist at Women’s College Hospital in Toronto, and co-author of the CMAJ commentary.
Dr. Sheryl Spithoff at Women's College Hospital says there should be more guardrails in place when it comes to privacy regulation and sensitive health data. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)
“It gives these companies significant discretion over using patient or individual data without consent.”
What is a ‘legitimate interest’?

Companies are required by the bill to document their legitimate interests, carry out privacy impact assessments to judge the risks to individuals and be able to provide this information on request. But Spithoff says companies should be required to inform regulators from the start and that this “legitimate interest” clause should only be for rare instances.
“Also there should be higher standards for sensitive information like personal health information,” she said.

The CMAJ commentary pointed out that the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation requires a high bar of proof and specifies that “legitimate interest” does not take precedence over the “fundamental freedoms and rights” of the data owners in question. Bill C-36 doesn’t provide these kinds of guardrails.

items: Canada's AI strategy aims to make health data more accessible. How will it protect privacy?
Judge orders Meta to pay $25B US for misleading consumers about data privacy

blocks.text: When CBC News asked AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office what counted as a “legitimate interest” and what safeguards were in place to prevent private health data from being sold to private-sector companies, the minister’s office repeated the definition given in the bill.

“Organizations relying on this exception would be subject to safeguards, including requirements to assess privacy risks and take steps to mitigate them,” the minister’s office said in a statement, without expanding on what those safeguards were.
'The moment is here' to modernize Canada's privacy laws: AI minister
Data sold to pharmaceutical companies

Last year, a study Spithoff worked on found that millions of Canadians’ health data, including details about their medical history and prescriptions, was being stripped of identifying material and then sold to pharmaceutical companies.

items: Millions of Canadians' health data available for sale to pharmaceutical industry, study shows

blocks.text: At the time, study authors warned that while this sharing of info could lead to better patient care, it also opened up the risk that private pharmaceutical companies could use this information to put their economic interests above the interest of patients and drive up prices.
Other jurisdictions are tackling similar privacy problems.

Earlier this year, a class-action lawsuit was launched against Chicago-based Tempus AI, alleging that after the company acquired a genetic testing firm, Ambry Genetics, they compelled the firm to hand over patients’ genetic and clinical data, trained their AI systems on it and sold that data to pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies without patients’ consent or knowledge.

Bill C-36 requires that personal information be "de-identified" by modifying personal details, like names and health card information. But researchers are concerned about the potential for re-identification as AI tools advance, where sensitive information could be linked back to specific individuals.

Teresa Scassa, the Canada Research Chair in Information Law at the University of Ottawa, says there's an increasing risk of de-identified data being traced back to individuals as AI tools grow more advanced. (CBC)

“There are very real concerns that nothing can be properly or fully anonymized anymore … with the amount of other data that's available and the power of AI technologies,” said Teresa Scassa, the Canada Research Chair in Information Law and Policy at the University of Ottawa and another author of the CMAJ commentary.
Scassa says that de-identified or even anonymized data can allow for correlations and links to be drawn that can affect individuals negatively even if they are not identified in those data sets.

She says individuals can be “profiled as somebody who is at a high risk of having a particular medical condition which would be expensive to treat, and therefore they might not be eligible for [types of] insurance.”
Under the proposed bill, deliberately re-identifying personal information would be an offence, but Scassa noted that this could be hard to prove.

Experts caution that even fully anonymized datasets can contain and amplify biases present in the health-care system, potentially putting patient information at risk. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
Anonymized data still carries risk
Critics are also concerned that the proposed legislation only covers information that has been de-identified — there’s no protection for what’s known as anonymized data.

According to the bill, de-identification means “modify[ing] personal information so that an individual cannot be directly identified from it, although a risk of the individual being identified remains.” Anonymized data, as defined in the bill, is data that has been “irreversibly and permanently” stripped of personal information so there is no “reasonably foreseeable” risk an individual can be identified.

items: After years of calls for data, study confirms Black Canadians face higher risk of maternal complications
Canadians' health data at risk of being handed over to U.S. authorities, experts warn

blocks.text: But experts warn anonymized data still contains risks, and say it’s the very data used to train AI systems.
“There are risks to the use of the information in artificial intelligence systems and we have no means of governing it,” said Scassa.

The commentary explains that anonymized data, which would fall outside of the scope of the law, often reflects societal biases that, when incorporated into AI systems, can lead to discrimination against people with shared characteristics.
Could AI help manage overcrowding in N.B. hospitals?
Authors provide an example of this discrimination in the U.S. when a widely used algorithm to allocate hospital resources was found to allocate fewer resources to Black people than white people.
“[Researchers] found out that it was because the algorithm was relying on past use of health system resources to allocate future resources,” said Spithoff.
Health data benefits

While experts say there are legitimate concerns over the use of sensitive health data, some other physicians are highlighting that when used safely, this information can be crucial in advancing health-care research.

Dr. Amol Verma is a physician and scientist at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto who leads a hospital research network called VITAL, which enables access to de-identified hospital data for health-care organizations nationally.
Dr. Amol Verma, with Unity Health Network's generative AI program, is pictured at St. Michael's Hospital, in Toronto, on Sept. 11, 2024. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
He says his network works with hospitals and with AI tools to make health data usable for research and innovation while still protecting patient privacy.
“We've been able to improve the efficiency of hospital care, reducing the time people spend in hospital safely, without causing increased risk to patients,” Verma said.
Verma said that concern over privacy is not necessarily a constraint on innovation.
“I think the only way we can have innovation around data in our health-care system is hand-in-hand with innovation and privacy protection.”

articles.title: These moms fought to change Canada's 'discriminatory' EI Act — and officially won
articles.summary: The legal battle is finally over for a group of six Quebec moms who fought to have certain provisions of the EI Act changed. The federal government says it will not challenge a Federal Court of…

image.caption: The federal government said it won't appeal a ruling by the Federal Court of Appeal that found it discriminatory to deny regular EI benefits to mothers who lost their jobs during, or shortly after, their maternity and parental leaves. (Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

The legal battle is finally over for a group of six Quebec moms who fought to have certain provisions of the EI Act changed. The federal government says it will not challenge a Federal Court of Appeal ruling in favour of the mothers who were denied job loss benefits after their maternity leaves.
Canada won't appeal ruling in favour of 6 Quebec women denied job loss benefits after mat leave
Relief, pride and tears. That's how Laurie Chalifour-Racine reacted when she learned a years-long legal battle over the Employment Insurance Act was finally over.
Chalifour-Racine was one of six Quebec moms who fought to have sections of the law struck down.
All six women lost their jobs during, or shortly after, their maternity and parental leaves and were subsequently denied regular Employment Insurance benefits as a result.
They argued the law was discriminatory and disproportionately affected women and, in September, the Federal Court of Appeal agreed, handing them a victory.
It was only last week, however, that the group learned the federal government would not challenge the ruling.
In an email to CBC News, the office of the minister of jobs and families confirmed the government would not appeal the court's decision, focusing instead on amending the legislation to align with it.

"The Government of Canada will work on solutions in [the] coming year to enhance the EI system to better reflect the needs of a modern workforce, including working parents, with flexible, reliable support," the email reads.
Laurie Chalifour-Racine with her two children Cayden, 10, seen standing in back, and Kenan, 8. (Submitted by Laurie Chalifour-Racine)
Chalifour-Racine says she's still coming to terms with what it all means.
"I feel relieved, I feel very proud," she said.
"I do feel that this will have a big impact on, you know, new mothers, women in general …. This is big."
Absence of job loss protection 'absolutely unfair'

Chalifour-Racine, the lead plaintiff in the case, was laid off 10 years ago, in December 2016, from her job at a Montreal-area financial institution. At the time, she was on maternity leave with her first-born.
She says she received a severance package from the employer which amounted to a few weeks of salary and called Service Canada to know if she would be eligible for EI job loss benefits.
She was denied on the grounds that she hadn't accrued enough insurable work hours in the last 52 weeks to qualify.
"Of course I wasn't working," she said. "Like, I was busy with my child that I was nursing and then, you know, no daycare and all of that."
Chalifour-Racine said even if her husband at the time was able to support her, it put the family under financial stress.

items: Federal Court of Appeal rules in favour of Quebec moms denied EI benefits after maternity job loss
She lost her job after her maternity leave. Now she's been denied EI

blocks.text: She was incredulous that in 2017, women could still find themselves without job loss protection when having children.
"When you get pregnant, nobody knows that you put yourself at risk," she said, adding she found the situation "absolutely unfair."

After numerous phone calls looking for advice, Chalifour-Racine eventually found help with Mouvement Action Chômage (MAC) de Montréal, an advocacy group dedicated to defending the rights of the unemployed.
Fight for equal rights

In 2018, lawyers with MAC de Montréal helped Chalifour-Racine and five other mothers who joined the cause bring their case to the Social Security Tribunal of Canada — an administrative tribunal that oversees disputes over the interpretation and application of laws and regulations.

Some of the women in the group were denied EI benefits because, like Chalifour-Racine, they hadn’t accumulated enough insurable work hours during the reference period, while others had maxed out their benefits.
The Employment Insurance Act limited the combination of regular job loss benefits and special benefits, such as maternity and parental leave, to 50 weeks.
In 2022, the general division of the tribunal ruled in the women's favour and agreed that parts of the EI Act violated their constitutional rights to equality under the law.
The Canada Employment Insurance Commission (CEIC), however, appealed the decision and subsequently won, prompting the group to bring the case to the Federal Court of Appeal.

The appellate court upheld the lower tribunal's decision, finding that the provisions in the EI Act that limit the stacking of maternity and parental benefits with job loss benefits, even if they apply to both men and women, disproportionately affect women.
The three-judge panel unanimously declared the discriminatory parts of the EI Act to be "of no force or effect," meaning they have been struck down, but suspended the declaration for one year.
Change needed sooner rather than later
Sibel Ataogul, the lead attorney for the applicants, called it a landmark case.
She said the Federal Court of Appeal's decision speaks to how the Act had been sexist toward women since its very beginnings.
At different times, women either couldn't receive benefits at all or were disqualified from receiving them depending on their marital status.
"So it is a landmark case insofar as that I think it really takes away that hopefully last sort of remaining element that was just really discriminatory against women," she said.
Ataogul said the responsible thing for the government to do now is ensure it makes the necessary changes as soon as possible so that women can get the benefits they are entitled to.
The court gave the government until Sept. 3, 2027 to amend the law.
Fanny Labelle with the Mac de Montréal said it is also hoping for a speedy process and, while the legal battle may be over, there is still a lot of work to do.
She said there are hundreds of women whose files at the Social Tribunal are on hold, pending the legislative changes and the way they will be applied.
She said the Mac de Montréal will continue to meet with legislators and push for the specific changes it wants to see.
The organization is also planning a big celebration to mark what it says is a collective win, not just for women in Quebec, but across Canada.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Annabelle Olivier is a digital journalist at CBC Montreal. She previously worked at Global News as an online producer. You can reach her at anne.isabelle.olivier@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary offer
articles.summary: The president told the Ultimate Fighting Championship boss to "please take the job" in a Truth Social post on Saturday.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.
Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".
It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."
White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.
On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".
"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.
"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.
"But, it was it was just a little fun."
The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job.
She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.
Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.
In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".
He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.
"Dana, please take the job!"
Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already".
"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.
White leads UFC, and PowerSlap , a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.
He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.
This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

articles.title: ‘Who is it for?’: Labor group questions ASEAN Summit’s toll on workers
articles.summary: DSWD has aided 30 Pasay vendors affected by security restrictions, but group says employees of affected businesses may also be losing wages.

blocks.text: November 9, 2026 | 4:41pm

MANILA, Philippines — A labor group has pressed the Department of Labor and Employment to identify the exact number of workers who've lost their income after preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit have temporarily shut businesses in Pasay City.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) announced Monday, November 9, that its initial assessment shows 30 displaced vendors or individuals, but Josua Mata, secretary general of the Sentro ng mga Nagkakaisa at Progresibong Manggagawa (SENTRO), raised the possibility that more have been affected.
The number of affected employees remain unclear, Mata said, as most reports had surfaced through workers' complaints on social media.

"[DOLE] should really clarify and investigate how many workers have been affected by this disruption [...] They should not wait for social media posts. They should be the ones looking," Mata said in Filipino in a radio interview with broadcasters Ted Failon and DJ Chacha on Monday, November 9.
The Philippines, which chairs ASEAN this year, will host the summit and related meetings at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay from November 15 to 18.
Malacañang declared those three days special non-working days across Metro Manila under Proclamation 1447 to ease traffic and secure summit participants.
SENTRO, however, has received information that some establishments in Pasay had been barred from operating as early as October 29, more than two weeks before the holidays begin.
The Pasay City government began partial road closures near summit venues on October 24, with full closures on designated roads running from Monday until November 20.
Summit is expected to draw Southeast Asia's presidents and world leaders such as United States President Donald Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Aid for 30 vendors

The DSWD confirmed several pares stalls and carinderias inside the Cultural Center of the Philippines complex, where the summit venue is located, were temporarily closed because of tightened security.

As compensation, the department said it would provide financial aid and family food packs to 30 affected vendors on the orders of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian.
"Based on the initial assessment, 30 individuals or vendors lost income there, and they will immediately receive cash assistance of not more than P10,000," DSWD spokesperson Irene Dumlao said Monday.
Mata however pointed out this cash assistance left out employees of the businesses that had been closed.

"Let me be very clear: we're not against ASEAN. But our question is, who is it for?" Mata said. "They cannot simply tell people to stop working, stop earning and let their families go hungry just so we can host ASEAN properly."

Under Labor Advisory No. 16, signed by Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino, the no-work, no-pay principle applies to employees who do not work on November 16 to 18, unless a company policy, practice or collective bargaining agreement provides otherwise.
Those who report for work are entitled to an extra 30% of their basic wage for the first eight hours, or 50% if the day falls on their rest day.
For a minimum-wage earner in Metro Manila (where the daily rate for non-agricultural workers rose to P755 in September), three unpaid days would amount to around P2,265 in lost wages.

Mata said the government declared the non-working holidays without consulting labor groups. Dialogue with DOLE had dwindled since SENTRO criticized Tolentino's handling of the latest Metro Manila wage orders, he said, referring to Wage Order NCR-27, which a Pasig court blocked, and NCR-28, which the regional wage board issued in its place.
"It's as if they're allergic to talking to us," Mata said.
Mata urged the officials behind the Metro Manila-wide holidays to call a dialogue immediately and, if needed, come up with a more targeted policy.
"Hindi ba napakalaking contradiction naman nito na nag-uusap sila tungkol sa prosperity ng ating rehiyon and yet namumulubi ang mga mamamayan natin just to host them?" he said.
(Isn't it a massive contradiction that they are discussing the prosperity of our region, while our own people are left destitute just to host them?)

articles.title: Turkey pushes for transition at COP31 as coal burns
articles.summary: The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.

image.caption: Solar energy capacity in Turkey has skyrocketed over the last decade, though coal power still dominates the gridImage: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Turkey welcomes delegates to the 2026 UN climate talks in Antalya and pushes for cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, it can point to surging renewable energy capacity at home.
The COP31 host has approved more than 33 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage projects since 2022 that can power over 27 million homes.
Among the largest battery project pipelines in Europe, this storage will complement fast-expanding wind and solar energy that today provides 22% of electricity in Turkey, up from 4.5% a decade ago.
Yet this clean energy upswing is a long way from compensating for the country's overreliance on fossil fuels.

Turkey's coal-fired electricity generation increased by roughly one-third in the last decade, and in 2024 overtook Germany and Poland, which previously had the highest coal power capacity in Europe before it began to decline.
UN climate summit opens amid worsening climate crisis
Coal undermining climate ambition
Turkey is among the few industrialized countries that has yet to commit to a phaseout date for coal — the fossil fuel with the highest planet-heating emissions.
Yet at the same time, "coal's position in the electricity market in Turkey is increasingly precarious," Efe Baysal, Turkey team lead at global environment network, 350.org, told DW.

He points to high local community opposition to coal projects on environmental grounds or due to lack of financial viability. According to German nonprofit climate campaigners, Beyond Fossil Fuels, some 97% of new coal projects have been cancelled in the last decade in Turkey, in what it calls "a global record."

"Turkey's coal project failure rate is the final nail in Europe's coal coffin," said Kasia Szeniawska of Beyond Fossil Fuels in a statement earlier this year. "Coal power is finished: it's financially risky, increases costs for billpayers, harms people's health, and sabotages climate goals."
But in June, Turkey announced plans to expand one of its largest coal plants and near double its capacity.

blocks.caption: COP31 host Turkey still relies on coal for electricity and has no plans to phase it outImage: Omer Urer/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The move underlines Turkey's "conservative energy policy" and "highly insufficient" climate goals, said Umit Sahin, head of the climate change program at the Istanbul Policy Center, a global research institute.

Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to keep rising until 2038, meaning it will struggle to meet its plans to reach net zero by 2053, notes Climate Action Tracker, a climate research think tank.
Push for electrification, energy independence

Aside from climate concerns, Turkey's high dependence on imported fossil energy makes it extremely vulnerable to volatile global oil and gas markets. The nation currently imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of crude oil and 60% of its coal — which together make up a "lion's share” of Turkey's energy capacity, said Baysal.
It is partly this dependence that has inspired Turkey's push for greater electrification at the COP31 climate conference.
In September, the country launched the "35x35" global electrification pledge, which aims to increase electrification of world economies from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The goal is for electrification to replace fossil fuels, including in transport, buildings and industry, and preferably using clean energy, though this is not mandatory —heat pumps, for example, emit fewer greenhouse gases than gas boilers, even when the electricity is generated using fossil fuels.
The pledge complements existing UN climate goals of doubling energy efficiency and tripling renewables to keep temperature rise in line with the Paris climate agreement.
Turkey's mining threatens ancient olive grove heritage
Turkey COP31 President Murat Kurum will promote the 35x35 pledge in Antalya on both climate and energy security grounds.

"[The war in the Gulf] has shown us, once again, that fossil fuels do not guarantee energy supply security," he said earlier this year at a UN climate meeting in Bonn, Germany. "Investment in alternative energy sources, in particular to support energy diversity, means stability, resilience and clean development."
But despite the rhetoric, Climate Action Tracker says that under Turkey's National Energy Plan, the COP31 host is only on track to electrify around 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.
Can renewables expansion turn the tide?
Turkey is one of numerous Mediterranean countries facing extreme climate impacts like wildfires and record heat, in addition to recent severe and deadly flooding.

blocks.caption: Torrential rainfall caused severe flash floods in Istanbul in OctoberImage: Adem Kutucu/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: As it hosts this year's climate summit, the country has a great opportunity to hasten the energy transition, said Baysal, especially since it receives nearly double the annual sunlight of Germany.
Turkey is already starting to realize some of this potential, with one analysis showing the country produces more solar module manufacturing capacity than several major European countries combined.
Solar increased from around 0.1% of total installed electricity capacity in 2014 to almost 21% at the beginning of 2026, according to Turkey's resources and energy ministry.

The COP31 host can reduce its emissions 35% by 2035 if 10 GW of solar and wind is added each interim year — as opposed to the government's target of 8 GW — noted Umit Sahin. This goal will be helped by fast-expanding battery capacity, he said.
"But if you don't phase out coal, your emissions cannot go down," he added.
Meanwhile, the COP presidency could be a "turning point" and "a very important step for Turkey," said Sahin.
If the country wants to show climate leadership, and reduce energy dependency, it will need to embrace a "progressive climate policy" that promotes a full energy transition, he added.
Serdar Vardar and Jonathan Rampley-Sturgeon contributed reporting to this article.
COP31 climate summit: What would count as success?

articles.title: At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
articles.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life

blocks.text: At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

articles.title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
articles.summary:
From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions,…

blocks.text: In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.

blocks.caption: Young people gather for a protest in Brussels, Belgium, last month. Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/Shutterstock

blocks.text: From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.

Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.

Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.

blocks.caption: Activists gather in Dhaka in 2024 to demand action after the deaths of students during anti-quota protests. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

blocks.text: The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.

Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.

blocks.caption: Serbian students cycle in Austria in 2025 during a bike ride to Strasbourg to publicise protests in their country. Photograph: Igor Pavićević/Reuters

blocks.text: Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.

Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.

“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.

blocks.caption: Tens of thousands of people march in protest against the government, rearmament, and the high cost of living in Rome last month during a national strike called by the USB trade union.  Photograph: Marco Di Gianvito/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.

That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.

blocks.caption: Young people at a rally in Belo Horizonte spell out Explode, the catchphrase of the Lula Army WhatsApp group in Brazil. Photograph: Tiago Rogero/The Guardian

blocks.text: On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.

Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.

blocks.caption: Young supporters of Zohran Mamdani cheer as he speaks after winning the Democratic mayoral primary in June 2025. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

blocks.text: It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.

In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A protester wearing a Batman mask holds a loudspeaker during a demonstration organised by Gen Z regelt in October 2026. Photograph: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

blocks.caption: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta party clash with police as they attempt to march toward India’s parliament to demand the resignation of the education minister in Delhi in July 2026. Photograph: Vipin/AP

blocks.text: Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.

It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.

blocks.caption: Police attempt to break up a protest in Paris this week. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP

blocks.text: In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.

In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.

blocks.caption: Protesters at a demonstration in Rabat, Morocco, in September 2025 calling for reforms in the public health and education sectors. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.

The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.

Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.

blocks.caption: Students from North Carolina A&T State University and UNC Greensboro march to polling places on the first day of early voting in Greensboro, North Carolina, on 15 October 2026. Photograph: Jamarious Simmons/Black Voters Matter Fund

blocks.text: As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.

Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

articles.title: ASEAN organizing council urges Filipinos to respect summit delegates
articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations Nations (ASEAN) Organizing Council on Monday urged Filipinos to respect foreign delegates expected to arrive in the country for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 3:56pm

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations Nations (ASEAN) Organizing Council on Monday urged Filipinos to respect foreign delegates expected to arrive in the country for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which the Philippines will host next week.

Retired Maj. Gen. Potenciano Camba, the council's deputy director general for operations, said more than 20 delegations are expected to attend the summit, including representatives from the 11 ASEAN member states.
The summit is scheduled for November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City.
The Philippines previously hosted the 48th ASEAN Summit and Related Meetings in May in Cebu.
Speaking on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon, Camba said security measures and traffic management plans were in place to ensure the safety of delegates and the public.
He acknowledged, however, that the public would have to adjust its daily routines because of expected disruptions during the event.

“We have informed our fellow Filipinos to adjust their daily routines. The MMDA, our partner under the Committee on Security, alongside local government units, has already issued a rerouting plan,” Camba said.

He also cited Proclamation No. 1447, which declared November 16, 17 and 18 as special non-working days in the National Capital Region to help ease traffic and ensure the safety of summit participants.

Addressing groups planning to stage demonstrations during the summit, Camba acknowledged their right to assemble but appealed to them to consider holding their protests after the country's hosting duties.
“Let us hear the voices of our countrymen. The Philippine National Police is fully prepared and capable of managing these situations," Camba said.
However, it would be much better if our fellow Filipinos held their protests after the summit because it would look bad if we have demonstrations while we have visitors,” he added.
Camba likened the situation to receiving guests at home, saying Filipinos should prepare for and show respect to their visitors.
The organizing council also said it was working with the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) to address potential cyberattacks and prevent the spread of misinformation.
Camba urged the public to share only verified information and refrain from spreading fake news during the summit.
He appealed for cooperation and the spirit of bayanihan to ensure the successful hosting of the regional gathering, saying the country's reputation was at stake.

The Philippines assumed the ASEAN chairmanship from Malaysia in 2026. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is expected to formally turn over the chairmanship to Singapore, which will host the bloc's summits in 2027.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Warden: Martin Romualdez's personal staff a regular visitor
articles.summary: The personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, Arvin de Guzman, gets to stay in the New Quezon City jail only during visiting hours, Jail Warden Lourdes Pacion said…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 3:56pm

The personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, Arvin de Guzman, gets to stay in the New Quezon City jail only during visiting hours, Jail Warden Lourdes Pacion said Monday.

Pacion made the clarification during the hearing on Romualdez’s whereabouts before the Sandiganbayan Third Division amid allegations of columnist Ramon Tulfo that the former speaker is able to leave the BJMP facility as he pleases in an ambulance, an allegation that Tulfo has since retracted for being false.
Romualdez, on the other hand, is in detention amid a P7.4 billion plunder charge leveled against him and three others over his alleged involvement in the flood control projects kickback scheme.
“Actually, the person allowed, he is a visitor. He is included in the visitor's list,” Pacion said.
This was different from Pacion’s earlier account where she said that he allowed Romualdez’s personal staff to stay with the lawmaker 24/7 due to Romualdez’s unstable mental health condition.
Asked by the court justices if De Guzman was allowed from 8 am to 5 pm inside the cell of Romualdez, Pacion answered yes.
“After visiting hours [of 8 am to 5 pm], he is on call 24/7,” Pacion added.
Pacion also apologized before the anti-graft court for saying that the personal staff of Romualdez is with the lawmaker 24/7.
“Sorry ‘your honor, siguro nataranta lang po ako your honor, pasensiya na po,” Pacion said.
(I am sorry. I was just flustered. I apologize.)

Romualdez’s legal counsel, Judd Roy, also confirmed before the Sandiganbayan that Romualdez’s legal team asked for the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to allow De Guzman, a longtime staff member of Romualdez, to assist the former Speaker with his medical needs.
Roy said De Guzman had worked for Romualdez for years and was familiar with his medical requirements, including the medications he needed to take. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.caption: Hundreds of synagogues were set on fire during the pogromsImage: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Commemorations are to be held nationwide to commemorate the Nazi pogroms of November 9-10, 1938, when mobs went on an antisemitic rampage, killing at least 91 Jewish people, ransacking Jewish businesses and burning down hundreds of synagogues.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to attend events in the eastern city of Weimar, where he is due to lay a wreath and hold a speech at the memorial site established at the site of the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald.
The Jüdische Gemeinde zu Berlin is to have all the names of Jewish Nazi victims read out over the day in commemoration of the pogroms.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be attending a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue in Munich, which was opened 68 years to the day after the main synagogue in the city was destroyed in the pogroms.
The pogroms are sometimes known as "Reichskristallnacht" or "Night of Broken Glass," but this name has fallen out of favor as underplaying the horrors of what happened.

articles.title: Solon calls for targeted, accessible housing finance programs
articles.summary: A member of the House committee on banks and financial intermediaries has called for targeted, accessible housing finance programs for middle- and lower-income first-time buyers to cushion the impact…

blocks.text: A member of the House committee on banks and financial intermediaries has called for targeted, accessible housing finance programs for middle- and lower-income first-time buyers to cushion the impact of prolonged monetary tightening.

Rep. JP Padiernos said policymakers should explore targeted financing assistance, more accessible housing loan terms, and stronger coordination among government agencies, housing finance institutions, and private developers.

He said that measures should be designed around the actual financing capacity of prospective homebuyers, with transparent loan terms and safeguards to ensure that monthly amortizations remain manageable and sustainable.

The lawmaker made the statement amid the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ 50-basis-point interest rate hike to 5.50%, which he said could further push homeownership out of reach for Filipino families, especially as credit terms tighten amid growing risks of stagflation in the country.
“For Filipino families, the central question is whether financing and housing options will remain attainable as monetary policy stays tight to combat inflation,” Padiernos said.
“For policymakers and the property sector, the immediate challenge is maintaining financial stability without completely closing the door on affordable homeownership,” he added.

He further said that higher borrowing costs add severe pressure to an already struggling residential property market, particularly amid concerns over slowing economic growth and persistent inflation, which could further constrain household purchasing power and access to housing finance..

S&P Global Ratings recently warned of the country’s worsening macroeconomic backdrop, pointing to a sharp slowdown in first-half 2026 GDP growth to just 2.6% alongside October inflation surging to a near four-year high of 7.8%. The rating agency projects full-year 2026 GDP growth to reach a modest 2.9%, with annual inflation averaging 5.5%.

With high oil prices and a strong El Niño pattern expected to drive food costs higher, S&P expects consumer spending to weaken further and squeeze household budgets through the first half of 2027. Consequently, the central bank is anticipated to keep interest rates higher for longer to contain persistent price pressures, even if supply-side relief eventually limits additional policy rate hikes.

“For families planning to buy a house or condominium through a bank loan, the BSP’s rate decision raises serious concerns about affordability, particularly as stagflationary pressures, rising food, electricity, fuel, and transportation costs, continue to erode household purchasing power,” said Padiernos.

While the BSP’s benchmark policy rate does not automatically yield an identical, immediate increase across all commercial housing loans, the lawmaker noted that higher benchmark rates directly influence banks’ underlying lending costs and repricing schedules.

“The BSP has an important role in maintaining price stability, which is essential to protecting the purchasing power of Filipino families. At the same time, we must examine complementary measures to ensure that higher borrowing costs do not further limit access to affordable housing,” Padiernos said.
“When mortgage rates escalate precisely as basic necessities consume a larger share of disposable income, homeownership becomes vastly more difficult to achieve,” he added.

The pressure on domestic real estate demand was evident even prior to the BSP's policy tightening. Data from real estate consulting firm Colliers Philippines revealed that net take-up of Metro Manila condominiums dropped to just 500 units in the second quarter of 2026, a 60% decline from the previous quarter and the lowest quarterly performance in five quarters.

Colliers also observed a clear shift toward lower-priced inventory: condominiums priced between P1.8 million and P3.6 million accounted for 67% of total net take-up in the first half of 2026, up from 33% in the same period last year. This trend underscores a tightening constraint on buyer affordability across Metro Manila.

To navigate the high-interest, high-inflation landscape, Colliers urged property developers to re-evaluate selling strategies and structure more flexible, extended payment arrangements, particularly for residential units priced between P2.5 million and P12 million. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Davao assessor unable to verify P6-M property in Sara's SALN
articles.summary: Duterte's defense establishes location match, but P6-million property link remains unclear.

blocks.text: November 9, 2026 | 3:28pm
Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin answers questions at the Senate impeachment court on Nov. 9, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The first defense witness in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial testified Monday, November 9 that two barangay names linked to her disputed property declarations refer to the same area in Davao City.

Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin said Barangay 74-A and Matina Crossing are the same area, potentially explaining a discrepancy in the location of properties listed in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

But when questioned about a property purchased by Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, for P6 million in 2024, Adalin said he could not say with certainty whether it was the same property listed in her SALN.

Duterte faces an impeachment allegation that she failed to fully disclose her assets and liabilities, including properties in Matina. While other charges against her have been dropped before the Senate impeachment court, she remains accused of unexplained wealth and discrepancies in her SALN.
During the defense's examination of Adalin, lawyer Lindon Baquel sought to establish that Barangay 74-A and Matina Crossing referred to the same location.
Benjamin Tolosa, counsel for the prosecution, said the prosecution panel was willing to stipulate that the document presented showed the two names referred to the same area.
The defense, however, preferred to have Adalin confirm this himself.
Questions over P6-M property

Tolosa later confronted Adalin with an Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration, or eCAR, dated July 2024, which showed that Carpio purchased a property for an actual selling price of P6 million.
Asked whether he could say with 100% certainty that the property covered by the transfer certificate of title, or TCT was the same property declared in Duterte's SALN, Adalin said he was uncertain.
Adalin explained that the subpoena issued to his office had asked him to verify a specific TCT.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero also questioned Adalin about the property records.

"If this honorable impeachment court would require us to submit or subpoena to submit all properties on by Attorney Manases (Carpio) in that particular barangay, then we will submit your honor," Adalin said.
Alleged failure to disclose. Article II of the Articles of Impeachment includes allegations that Duterte failed to fully disclose her assets and liabilities, including properties in Barangay Matina.
In October, a witness from the Land Registration Authority identified a 379-square-meter lot in Matina that Carpio purchased for P6 million in 2024.
The witness testified that the property did not match any entry in Duterte's 2025 SALN based on its price, location or mode of acquisition.
